Kulacūḍāmaṇi Nigama, edited by Arthur Avalon.
Homage to Śiva and Śivā.
The Kula-cūḍāmaṇi Tantra, Chapter One.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Goddess Tripurā is infinite; Kālikā is also infinite;
likewise Vāgīśvarī is infinite, as is Sukulākulā. (1)
Mātāṅginī, as well as Pūrṇā, Vimalā, Caṇḍanāyikā, Tripura, Ekajaṭā, Durgā, and she who is Kulasundarī. (2)
The Vaiṣṇava, the Gāṇapatya, and likewise the Mahāsaura doctrine;
the Śaiva, that which is born of Śaṅkara, and whatever else originates from the elements (bhūtas). || 3 ||
"And the sixty-four tantras, which are the most excellent of the Mothers" (1.13).
Following this, in the Vāmakeśvaratantra, beginning with "the Mahāmāyāśambara," the names of the sixty-four tantras are stated; however, the reading there differs slightly here and there.
This reading is observed to be maintained and explained as both authentic and accepted by the great community of scholars. Furthermore:
"The Mahāmāyā-śambara, the Jāla-śambara of the Yogins, and the Tattva-śambara."
And also the Bhairavāṣṭaka.

In the first half [of this list], there are four tantras: Mahāmāyā (1), Śambara (2), Yoginījāla (3), and the forms of Śambara (4). The double mention of Śambara is to be explained as referring to both the Śambara and the Bṛhat-Śambara. Some, however, explain it as the Yoginītantra and the Jālaśambara.

There are six tantras: the *Tattvaśambara*, which is one, and another, the *Bhairavāṣṭaka*; these two are mentioned in the latter half [of the verse]. Furthermore, there are the supreme Mothers of the tantras:
the *Mahāsārasvata* and the *Mahāmāyāśambara*, as well as Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, and Krodha.
Unmatta, Kapāla, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra—these are the eight Bhairavas.
Thus, the Tantra concerning the eight Bhairavas is renowned by the name *Bhairavāṣṭaka*.
Furthermore, there is the *Bahurūpāṣṭaka*, the *Yāmalāṣṭaka*, the *Candrajñāna*, the *Vāsuki*,
and likewise the *Mahāsaṃmohana*.

The eight *Bahurūpa* Tantras are those named after the seven Mothers along with Śivadūtī; these seven Saṃhitās of the Bahurūpāṣṭaka are designated by the name *Bahurūpatantra*. The eight *Yāmalas* are: (1) Brahmayāmala, (2) Viṣṇuyāmala, (3) Rudrayāmala, (4) Lakṣmīyāmala, and (5) Umāyāmala.
The *Skandayāmala* (6), the *Gaṇeśayāmala* (7), and the *Grahayāmala* (8)—thus numbering eight.

However, Bhāskara recited the *Jayadrathayāmala* in place of the *Grahayāmala*. In this verse, nineteen tantras are mentioned, including the three: the *Candrajñāna*, the *Vāsuki*, and the *Mahāsaṃmohana*.
O Mahādeva! [I have received] the Mahocchuṣya, the Vātula, the Vātulottara, the Hṛdbheḍa, the Tantrabheḍa, the Guhyatantra, and the Kāmika.
The Kalāvāda, the Kalāsāra, and likewise the Kubjikāmata; the Tantrottara, the one called Vīṇā, the Trotala, and the Trotalottara.
The *Pañcāmṛta*, the *Rūpabheda*, the *Bhūtoḍḍāmara*, the *Kulasāra*, the *Kuloḍḍīśa*,
and likewise the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
O God! [I have taught] the Sarvajñānottara, as well as the Mahākālīmata, the Mahālakṣmīmata, and the Siddhayogeśvarīmata.
The Kuruṣikāmata, the Devarūpikāmata,
the Sarvavīramata, and the supreme Vimalāmata.

In this [work], twenty-eight tantras are enumerated by means of these five verses, as follows: (1) Mahocchuṣma, (2) Vātula, (3) Vātulottara, (4) Hṛdbheḍa, (5) Tantrabheḍa, (6) Guhyatantra, (7) Kāmika, (8) Kalāvāda, (9) Kalāsāra, (10) Kubjikāmata, and (11) Tantrottara.
(12) the one called Vīṇā (Vīṇātantra), (13) Trotala, (14) Trotalottara, (15) Pañcāmṛta, (16) Rūpabheda, (17) Bhūtoḍḍāmara, (18) Kulasāra, (19) Kuloḍḍīśa,
(20) Kulacūḍāmaṇi, (21) Sarvajñānottara, and (22) Mahākālīmata.

The Mahālakṣmīmata (23), the Siddhayogeśvarīmata (24), the Kurūpikāmata (25), the Devarūpikāmata (26), the Sarvavīramata (27), and the Vimalāmata (28). These are the Eastern, Western, Southern, Northern, and Unsurpassed [Tantras].
The Tantra, the Vaiśeṣika knowledge, the Vīrābali, and the Ratha—these are the others.
Aruṇeśa, Mohinīśa, and Viśuddheśvara as well.
By this half-verse, eleven tantras are mentioned,
namely: (1) Pūrvāmnāya, (2) Paścimāmnāya, (3) Dakṣiṇāmnāya, (4) Uttarāmnāya, (5) Niruttaratantra, (6) Vaiśeṣikatantra, and (7) Jñānārṇavatantra.
The *Vīrābalitantra* (8), the *Aruṇeśatantra* (9), the *Mohinīśatantra* (10),

and the *Viśuddheśvaratantra* (11)— among these sixty-four Tantras that primarily focus on Śakti, it is intended that these [four] should be known as the most excellent and supreme. And thus, for the yogins...
The Jālaśambara [spell]. || 4 ||
The *Tattvaśambaraka*, the *Bhairavāṣṭaka*,
the knowledge of the *Bahurūpāṣṭaka*, and the *Yāmalāṣṭaka* as well; (5)
O Great Goddess! [The Tantras are] Tantrajñāna, Vāsuki, Mahāsaṃmohana, Mahāsūkṣma, Vāhana, and Vāhanottara [as well as Mahāsāṃkhya, Mahādeva, Vātula, and Vātulottara]. || 6 ||
The *Hṛdbhe-da*, the *Mātṛbhe-da*, the secret reality (*guhyatattva*) of the *Kāmika*,
the *Kalāvāda*, the *Kalāsāra*, and likewise another, the *Kubjikāmata*. (7)
And Māyottara, the one called Vīṇā, Trotala, Trotalottara, Pañcāmṛta, Rūpabheda, and Bhūtaḍāmara as well. (8)
O Goddess, just as the Kulasāra and the Kuloḍḍīśa Tantra are the soul of the universe,
so too is the Mahāpitṛmata the essence of all knowledge.
O Goddess! the Mahālakṣmīmata, the Siddhayogeśvarīmata, the Kurūpikāmata, O Goddess! and also the Rūpikāmata; || 10 ||
O Goddess! This is the doctrine of all heroes, the supreme Vimalāmata;
it is eastern, western, southern, northern, and unsurpassed.
The Tantra-vaiśeṣika-jñāna, and then another, the Śivābali;
Aruṇeśa, Mohaneśa, and Viśuddheśvara as well. || 12 ||
"O Goddess Bhairavī! Having heard these tantras and likewise others by the millions, you have not found joy anywhere. (13)
Tell me then, O lady of beautiful hips, how [this can be] while I am at your feet?
The Goddess said:
Listen, O God! O Supreme Bliss, whose nature is the supreme lineage (parākula), you who are the ocean of the Kula [tradition] and the knowledge of all Tantras sealed by my Māyā. 15.
If I am Prakṛti, whose ultimate resort is consciousness and bliss,
then where is Brahmā, where is Hari, where is Śambhu, where is the god, and where is the recitation of Manu?
Where is creation, or where is preservation, and where is the stage of dissolution?
Where is passion, where is pleasure or pain, where is liberation, and where is virtue? (17)
"Where is faith, and where is atheism? Where is the status of a teacher, and where is that of a disciple?
Having concealed her true self through illusion, she has become threefold and is intent upon me. (18)
She delights in the intoxication of the flavor of the external world and is subject to transformation;
she is the five elements, the subtle bodies (liṅgas), and the one hundred and one [channels]. 19.
The manifestation of the nature of the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, beginning with Brahmā, was born.
All things manifest here; from that arises the conceptualization of existence and so forth. (20)
Through the differentiation of Śiva and Śakti, the emergence of the qualities (guṇas) arises;
all of you, beginning with Brahmā, are my portions born of [my] being.
Inseparable from one another and filled with tantras and mantras,
though cherished by the state of nirvāṇa, I shall cause them to attain death.
Furthermore, these manifest from the Puruṣa who is beyond Prakṛti:
the ego (ahaṃkāra), the five subtle elements (mātrās), and then sattva, rajas, and tamas. (23)
This entire universe, consisting of these [elements], perishes and yet manifests again. Having known that this world consists of these principles, one becomes a true celibate student (brahmacārī).
O Omniscient One, if you know me, where is there any need for sacred tradition (āmnāya) or for officiating at sacrifices (yājana)? 24.
O Omniscient One! If you do not know me, then where is the sacred tradition (Āmnāya) and where is the performance of sacrifice?
For I have assumed the form of a woman—the very essence of creation, whose nature is identical to mine.
I have exerted myself to know you, the Guru established in the yoga of existence;
yet even by this much, O Lord of Gods, the reality of my [nature] is not realized. (26)
The Goddess said:
Listen, my son, you who are skilled in the service of supreme bliss;
I shall now describe the means for those whose practice is liberated from yoga.
It is the sole essence of all tantras, saluted by all the gods;
it is the secret that bestows all omniscience and awakens the realization of reality. || 28 ||
O child! It is worthy of destroying both sin and merit, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, consisting of every wonder, and enchanting even the learned. (29)
O wise one, [this] knowledge gives rise to manifold meanings; it is crowded and agitated by manifold meanings;
it is fully understood by true teachers and is the supreme refuge for excellent disciples. (30)
That which is the conduct of all speakers yet is censured by all speakers,
was not told by me to Viṣṇu, nor to Dhātṛ, nor to Gaṇapa.
(5) But you must preserve with effort that which is to be hidden in the heart.
O child! Without this tantra, there is no authority [even for the gods]. 32.
O child! Likewise, I shall now describe the purification of knowledge according to the family tradition (kulācāra).
Having risen early in the morning, the practitioner should bow down to the family tree (kulavṛkṣa).
Having meditated upon the Kula from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should remember the Guru named Prahlādānandanātha and also Sanakānanda.
Kumārānandanātha, Vasiṣṭhānandanātha, Krodhānanda, Sukhānanda, and after that, Jñānānanda. (35)
Then, having worshipped the bliss of awakening, one should meditate upon the Kula above;
their eyes are the bliss of the heart, overflowing with the delight of the essence of the Great Essence (mahārasa).
They have completely crushed and pulverized all darkness through the embrace of their spiritual family;
they are intent upon their inner hearts being filled with compassion for their noble disciples. || 37 ||
Having thus bowed to the Kula-guru, who possesses the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness and who knows the meaning of all the Kula Tantras, and having dismissed the Kula-mātṛkā; 38.
Embracing one's own family station, one should resort to a sacred bathing place for the purpose of purification; O child! A Śākta Kulaguru has been described as bringing happiness. (39)
O child! This wondrous secret must be guarded in times of danger from the uninitiated (paśu).
Those who, though Śāktas and followers of the Kula, abandon the Lord of the Kula (kulanātha) to serve others (parasevinaḥ), [are lost]. (40)
For them, both initiation and sacrifice lead only to malevolent magic;
therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in a guru of noble lineage. || 41 ||
One of noble birth is proclaimed to be qualified for all sciences;
he alone, and no other, is the master of initiation for every mantra in this world. (42)
Thus ends the first chapter in the Kulacūḍāmaṇi Tantra.
The second chapter. The Goddess said:
Now, O child, I shall explain to you the bath that brings about the welfare of the Kula.
My forms are black, red, yellow, blue, and various others. || 1 ||
In that regard, the disciple who belongs to a particular lineage, perceiving himself as being of that very form,
[perceives] the entire heaven, the earth, and the netherworld (pātāla) where beings originate.
Having sipped water with *darbha* grass from his family lineage, he should likewise place *darbha*, flowers of his lineage, *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds, and water into the vessel of his lineage.
Having taken hold [of the materials], one should perform a bath for the pleasure of the family deity (kuladeva).
Having first made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should place the family-circle (kulacakra) in the water.
Having brought the root of the family together with the family-seal-hook (kulamudrāṅkuśa),
one should likewise invoke the family-sacred sites (kulatīrthas) right there, as well as that which consists of the family (kulātmaka).
Then, having drunk that water three times and performed the sprinkling of the body three times,
one should offer the *arghya* three times to the deity who is the root of the *kula*.
One should satisfy the gods, the ancestors, and the sages with the water of one's lineage;
then, having meditated upon those whose nature is the lineage, one should gratify the family deities.
In this very Bhairavītantra, their designation is also found:
"for the god Bhairava" and "by the agent Bhairava. (8)
Having first uttered the mantra known as Bhairava, one should then bestow [the initiation],
including the giver, the gift, and the recipient, in accordance with the specific form of the *liṅga*.
One should contemplate Bhairavī as being entirely identical in nature to Bhairava, during ancestral rites, weddings, acts of giving, ritual bathing, and the worship of the limbs [of the deity]. (10)
"O Lord, when you are thus intent on such thought, I am undoubtedly pleased;
then, being satisfied, I truly gladden all those worlds. (11)

Having risen and put on two garments of his family's style, and having applied the sectarian mark (tilaka) according to his lineage and form, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and complete the rite. || 12 ||
Having ascended the family throne (kulapīṭha), one performs the complete worship of the family deity (kuladeva).
Then, at the entrance, he is gratified by songs, dances, musical instruments, and so forth. (13)
Having removed that which has become a family [having recited it], one should worship the place of the family;
then, having cast away the family-seat, one should honor it as one pleases.

Then, having assumed the *kulāsana* posture according to the sequence of worshiping the Guru, one should perform purification through the distinctions of self-purification (*ātmaśuddhi*), ground-purification (*bhūmiśuddhi*), and body-purification (*dehaśuddhi*). (Alternatively: self-purification, seat-purification, and the distinctions beginning with body-purification. || 15 ||
Having offered the arghya, the wise man should then perform the specific rites of the family,
together with initiated, virtuous, young women who are devoted to their families.
Various kinds of flowers and diverse perfumes were gathered upon the sacrificial grounds by those devoted to the deities and their gurus. (17)
Camphor, nutmeg, incense, and other perfumes, as well as scented cloth, betel leaf, materials for offerings, and whatever incense, lamps, and so forth there may be—[these are to be provided]. 18.
Then the weaver, adorned with all kinds of ornaments and decorations,
should sprinkle the image with water consecrated by the recitation of the root-mantra and then install it.
One should place everything on one's own right side and set the *arghya* offering on the left;
furthermore, one should keep the materials of one's spiritual lineage (*kuladravya*) to the west of the deity.
With substances produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, with the *svayaṃbhū* flower and other flowers, with yellow pigment (*rocanā*), lac, red dyes, saffron, and reddish sandalwood. || 21 ||
Having fashioned the yantra and performed worship there, one should perform the recitation (or begin the recitation).
Having recited the mantra according to one's capacity and praised the Goddess, one should dismiss her. 22.
Having circumambulated those various women, whether his own or others,
he should first offer the full nectar-essence of the lineage to the Guru. (23)
But for a woman, she should apply the remainder within her own self;
she should maintain the application of the yantra in the secret place of the *brahmarandhra*.
It should not be given to atheists, nor to fools, nor to animals, nor to an enemy;
it should be given to one of noble birth, or else into the midst of water.
Then, meditating "I am He," being intent on the conduct prescribed for Vaiṣṇavas, his heart was filled with devotion to the name of Hari, and his actions were imbued with grace. || 26 ||
Like a thief, he should always enter alone, avoiding any delay through social attachment;
then, when only one watch of the night has passed, the man should go to the family home. (27)
Remaining in the midst of a couch of flowers, the one devoted to the Kula [should place] the Kula-yantro,
filled with the name of the target, within the Kula-cakraka.
Having marked it with his own name today, he should perform the family tradition;
by his own power, the practitioner brings forth the supreme power.
And listen with a concentrated mind, my child, to the attraction of another's power:
having brought back one's own beloved wife, who is virtuous and of great renown. (30)
Having obtained a guru devoted to his own lineage, one should initiate him with the Kula initiation,
[using] a virtuous woman born of the Kula whose eyes are rolling from the essence of supreme bliss.
The wise preceptor, his mouth filled with a morsel of betel-leaf and having protected himself on all sides,
should write [the mantra] upon the forehead of the disciple as if he were his own daughter.
One should draw the wheel of power (śakticakra) with three rotations, and then [draw] the Kāmakalā;
in its center, one should place the mantra, marked with the name and adorned with darbha grass.
There, having invoked the Goddess, meditated upon her, and worshipped her,
he then [recited] into the ear of that image the [mantra] accompanied by the seer and the meter.
Having recited the root mantra three times, he should whisper it into her left ear:
"From this day forward, O daughter, you shall be devoted to the worship and veneration of the Kula. (35)
Having taken the command from a woman of low family, free from shame and laziness, bring her to my subjugation according to the prescribed ritual. 36.
Having thus obtained permission from the guru, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff, saying:
"Save me, O Lord! O leader of the lotus-clan of the Kula tradition! (37)
"O you whose wealth is fame! Place the shade of your lotus-feet upon my head.
Having given the teacher his fee, she, whose eyes were reddened by betel-juice, [spoke thus]. (38)
Having elevated one's own family (kula) to the status of the supreme, one should perform the practice as desired;
however, in the worship of the limbs and enclosures (aṅgāvaraṇa-pūjā) and so forth, if one's own family is not deemed sufficient, [one may proceed otherwise]. 39.

Then, having meditated on the Guru at the crown of the head and having gratified the Kula with the essence of the nectar of the Kula, one should then meditate on the deity and recite the mantra without distraction. || 40 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the Kulacūḍāmaṇi Tantra.
The third chapter begins: The Goddess said:
Then, at that time of night, his own family was situated nearby on the left side upon a mattress [or upon the ground], adorned with red garments. (1)
Richly adorned with ornaments of gold, decorated with red perfumes,
and surrounded by fragrances, flowers, incense, and lamps, it was exceedingly beautiful.
Richly adorned with every kind of erotic ornament, her tremulous eyes sparkling;
she has surpassed the pair of nectar-filled breasts [or the immeasurable frontal globes] of the great elephant.
Having drawn a yantra on the forehead, containing the name of the person to be accomplished within it,
she placed her arm upon his shoulder in a graceful manner, her breasts resting against him.
Having performed the *japa* of *kūlākula*, one brings that family— whose mouths are filled with betel and who are intent upon it— instantly.
The yantra written with someone's name brings that person from as far as a hundred yojanas away, even if they are situated between rivers and mountains, at that very moment.
She was guarded by fetters and other restraints across thousands of other islands;
her waist was agitated by the weight of her breasts, and her eyes were tremulous.
Her shimmering orb of hips was revealed by her loosened girdle;
her heart longed for the practitioner, as she crept toward the entrance of the cave.
Within the opening of a wall reinforced with iron door-panels,
she was like a goddess moving about while seated within the presence of the practitioner.
O Mahādeva, at that very moment the practitioner brings her under his control;
if the practitioner is a Kaulika, such is the accomplishment of attraction.
(11) If there is no initiated woman, how can there be worship of the *kula*?
O child, if there is no worship of the *kula*, the *kula*-mantras turn their faces away [from the worship].
O child, when another woman herself becomes her guru, one should bestow the supreme [initiation] into her left ear and consecrate her with the mantra alone. || 12 ||
Listen to the mantra, O Mahādeva! I shall explain it to you exactly as it is:
the word *tripurāyai* at the end of *vānta* (vam) is proclaimed to be the Heart-mantra. (13)
This power (śakti) at the end of the word is called the purifying step;
then one should give the word for the Guru, and after that, the word for my Śakti.
"Kuru svāhā"—this mantra consists of twenty-six syllables;
O Lord, one should perform the purification of Śakti with this mantra. (15)
O most formidable one, through consecration (abhiṣeka), purification occurs even for a widow;
likewise for a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, or a Śūdrā who is an ornament of the Kula.
The Vaiśya woman, the barber’s daughter, the washerwoman, and likewise the Yoginī—all of these were noble women endowed with exceptional skill. (17)
At a crossroads, or by a river, at the foot of a bilva tree, or on a trident;
in a cemetery, at the foot of a bilva tree, in a marketplace, or in a royal palace. (18)
One should draw a large yantra with vermilion, containing the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) within it;
having worshipped there according to the rules with the essence of the Kula, one should worship the Kula.

Having gratified that which resides within it, one should then recite the mantra at night while moving about; one should worship it with devotion at night, for then, by the offering of a hundred thousand [recitations], they indeed become bestowers of success.
At the time of the *puraścaraṇa* rite, having honored another’s wife who has been initiated with garments, flowers, and the like, as well as with foods consisting of milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
At the time of the commencement, he himself partook of cooked food that was prepared and certain,
as well as various kinds of flour-cakes endowed with diverse flavors.
Milk, curd, clarified butter, buttermilk, fresh butter with sugar, powdered rock-salt, and various kinds of elixirs; (23)
Coconut, wood-apple, ginger, karamardaka [and orange, sudarśana], flat bean, citron, and the pomegranate fruit [the most excellent fruit]. || 24 ||
Various delightful fruits, various perfumes and ointments, sandalwood, musk, śrīkhaṇḍa, and fresh sprouts [from the celestial tree]. || 25 ||
It was made of taṅkana and lodhra, as well as water-born and forest-born materials;
it was produced from various mountains and adorned with various ornaments. [It was symmetrical. 26.
Having brought [the disciple] into an empty house and purified him with arghya water,
one should perform the rite of making [him] nectar (amṛtīkaraṇa) and lead him toward the Śaktis.
Having observed the eightfold manifestation of the forms of the maidens and their acts of self-identification, they were given names corresponding to the eight powers beginning with Brahmāṇī. (28)
Having first offered a seat and then once again a welcome,
one should likewise offer water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), drinking water, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and water. (29)
One should bathe [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and likewise perform the grooming of the hair;
having then incensed the hair, one should offer silk cloth.
Then, having spread a seat in another place and placed a pair of sandals there,
he brought [the deity] to that spot and adorned him with various ornaments and decorations.
Having adorned them with ointments, one should offer fragrances and garlands;
having invoked each respective power (śakti), one should bring it into union with their heads. || 32 ||
One should present the food—consisting of that which is to be chewed, sucked, licked, drunk, eaten, and consumed—in a beautiful golden vessel in the center of the pavilion. (33)
If they there are uninitiated, then one should present the Māyā-mantra;
then, one should recite the hymn into their left ears.
O Mother Goddess! Salutations to you! O sinless one who bears the form of Brahman!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me spiritual success. || 35 ||
O Maheśī! O boon-granting goddess! O you whose form is supreme bliss!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and bestow upon me spiritual accomplishment. || 36 ||
O Kaumāri, sovereign of all vidyās, O excellent one who sports as a maiden!
[Grant] by your grace... || 37 ||
O Goddess who bears the form of Viṣṇu, O you whose vehicle is the son of Vinatā! By your grace... [38]
O Vārāhī! O boon-granting Goddess! O You who lifted the earth with Your tusk!
Through Your compassion... [39]
O Goddess who bears the form of Śakra! O you who are worshipped by the gods beginning with Śakra [and worshipped by the Gaṇas]!
Out of compassion... || 40 ||
O Cāmuṇḍā! O you who are smeared with garlands of severed heads and blood! O destroyer of fear!
[Grant] by your grace... || 41 ||
O Mahālakṣmī! O you who remove the agitation and torment of great delusion! Out of compassion... [grant me]... || 42 ||
O Goddess, who consist of measure and measurer! O Goddess, who are beyond measure and measurer!
O Goddess, who are one yet manifold! O Goddess, whose form is the universe! Salutations be unto you! 43.
Whoever, being self-restrained, recites this hymn at the commencement of undertakings, or upon seeing a clever woman, for him no obstacle shall arise. (44)
O my son! These have been declared to you as the door-deities of one of noble lineage;
if one does not worship them at the time of initiation or during the occasion of daily worship, [the rite is flawed]. (45)
"O child! The fruit of his worship is carried away by yakṣas and rākṣasas.
Thus ends the Karṇejapa-stotra.
If they are overcome by shame, one should feed them outside of the house.

Having remained [in that state], one should recite the hymn of praise until satisfaction arises. Having sipped water for purification (ācamana), one should offer mouth-fresheners such as betel leaf and the like. (47)
Then one should offer again a garland smeared with fragrant sandalwood paste;
having paid homage, [dismissed [the deity], and performed circumambulation], and having indeed dismissed [the deity] and obtained the boon, one shall become happy. || 48 ||
If no other women go— neither one's own daughter, nor one's younger sister, nor an elder sister, nor a maternal aunt, nor one's mother, nor her co-wife (49)— then [one may approach].
Whether inferior or superior in age or by birth, the highest arts are to be honored by all those of noble lineage who have abandoned their own egoism.
Even when none of these are present, one [of them] should be worshipped with effort—whether she be consecrated or unconsecrated, a mother, or even a destitute woman. (51)
In the absence of the former, the latter should be worshipped, for there are countless women who are portions of my own self;
O Bhairava, if there is even one person who knows the Kula scriptures, he is worthy of worship therein.
All the gods, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others [as well as Satya, Brahmā, the Suras, and so forth], are indeed worthy of worship;
yet, if even a single young woman there is worshipped and beheld, [all are honored].
O Kulabhairava! All the supreme goddesses have indeed been worshipped—at the beginning, at the end, and in the middle—and especially upon the completion of the hundred thousand recitations.
If one does not honor one's beloved, then one is beset by obstacles;
there is no fruit from what was previously earned—what need is there to speak of another birth? 55.
Therefore, if one desires one's own welfare, as well as the pacification of my own heat of anger and the destruction of obstacles, one should strive with every effort. (56)
People of both noble and ignoble birth should be honored with effort, whether by oneself upon rising in the morning for the sake of worship, or again at the time of bathing. (57)
Whether they be refined or unrefined, O son, or even born of low lineage, they are to be saluted by all castes, noble and base alike, in the worship of the family. (58)
Even during the time of *puraścaraṇa*, if there should be a vision of a sacred seat (*pīṭha*), then the worship of that seat is not omitted, even if only mentally. (59)
O Bhairava! [I bow to] the highly fortunate one at Devīkūṭa, at Uḍḍīyāna, Yoganidrā at Kāmarūpa, and Mahiṣāsuramardinī. (60)
Kātyāyanī in Kāmabhūmi, she who is named Kāmā and bestows all desires;
Pūrṇeśī in Jālandhara, and Caṇḍikā on Mount Pūrṇa.
The goddess Kāmarūpā, who dwells in the cardinal directions, should be worshipped at Ṭhehāra;
or else, if by good fortune one beholds Kāmarūpa itself. (62)
Then, the worship of the vulva and other parts of the goddesses such as Durgā is performed there;
thereafter, having meditated upon the Kulanātha, one with an undistracted mind— || 63 ||
O child! One should complete the remainder preceded by the recollection of that [deity].
At the time of worship, one’s own wife, even if born of a low caste, should be employed with great effort.
They should be worshipped with diligent effort, and one should avoid duplicity therein;
for just as Viṣṇu is the supreme protector, so too is Śambhu the Lord. (65)
Just as the lotus-born Brahmā, or those twice-born ones headed by Vyāsa, as well as all the world-protectors beginning with Indra, along with the Gandharvas and Kinnaras; || 66 ||
The Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and others—the Guhyakas, Cāraṇas, and Khecaras—have kept secret that which was spoken by you, originating from the Śāstras. (67)
Likewise, you yourself must protect this family tradition which is so very difficult to find. || 68 ||
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇitantra*.
The fourth chapter begins with the Goddess saying:

Listen, my son! To this secret of mine arising from the conduct of the observance (samayācāra), devoid of which even thousands of millions of lineages do not attain success even in hundreds of millions of births. || 1 ||
That man, noble-minded and devoted everywhere to the conduct of Vaiṣṇavas, followed the family scriptures and the traditional practices of his lineage. || 2 ||
One should be patient with the censure of others and always intent on doing good;
whether on a mountain, in a forest, in a temple, or in a solitary, empty pavilion.
If by chance one should find oneself at a crossroads or in the middle of water,
one should meditate for a moment, recite the mantra, bow down, and then proceed as one pleases.
Having observed a vulture, one should offer salutation to Mahākālī unobserved;
likewise, having observed a jackal, the messenger of Yama, one should salute Kṣemaṅkarī.
O Kurarī! O Śyenī! O Kākī! O Kṛṣṇamārjārī!
O Pūrṇodarī! O Mahācaṇḍā! O Muktakeśī! O Balipriyā! (6)
O you whose face is pleased by the conduct of noble families! Salutations to you, beloved of Śaṅkara!
Having seen the cremation ground and the corpse, he followed it while circumambulating.
Having prostrated with this mantra, the practitioner of mantra shall attain happiness:
"O you of terrible fangs! O you of harsh eyes! O you who utter the sound 'kiṭi'! (8)
O Mother, dweller on the funeral pyre, salutations to you who possess a most terrible roar and cause a most terrible sound!
Having beheld her, whose nature is Tripura, wearing red garments and adorned with black flowers and red flowers,
one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground while reciting this mantra of praise.
O Tripurā, who resembles the bandhūka flower! O destroyer of fear! || 10 ||
O you born of the dawning of fortune! Homage to you, O lady of excellent complexion!
[To her who is] dark-complexioned [clad in dark garments and adorned with dark flowers], as well as to the flower and the king.
The little prince. || 11 ||
Having seen the elephants, horses, chariots, and weapons; the shield [and heroic men]; the heroic man; the buffalo and the family deity; and having seen the slayer of Mahiṣa (Mahiṣamardinī). || 12 ||

Having bowed to Jayadurgā, he is not tainted by obstacles. "Victory to you, O Goddess! O Mother of the World! O Slayer of Mahiṣa, salutations be unto you! O Mother of Tripura, O Goddess of the Three Deities!
Having beheld a vessel of wine, fish, meat, or a beautiful woman— || 14 ||
And having seen the goddess Bhairavī and having prostrated, one should contemplate the mantra for the destruction of terrible obstacles and for the fulfillment of the kula-conduct. 15.
I bow to you, O goddess who grants boons! Adorned with a garland of severed heads, with a face drenched in streams of blood, I pay homage to you. 16.
O Goddess who removes all obstacles! Salutations to you, O beloved of Hara!
O child, if these [beings] do not act with enmity upon seeing him, yet he proceeds placing the Śakti-mantra at the forefront, his success will not arise. (17)
If these [enemies] are subjected to killing, expulsion, or injury by means of snares and the like, how can that evil-minded person be my devotee? (18)
These, beloved of the noble families [the refuge of people], have arisen from a portion of Pradhāna;
likewise, hear, O Bhairava, that all the Ḍākinīs are portions of myself! (19)
If, through the union with attained siddhi, there is violence toward the ḍākinīs—
or even toward the dānavas, especially those devoted to me,
or toward the vaṭukas and bhairavas— then his siddhi shall not arise. (20)
Whether in a village, a city, a marketplace, or even at a crossroads,
whatever [object] a young woman beholds, she becomes free from her previous defects.
With her heart uniquely pierced by emotion, she gazed with a sidelong glance,
appearing like a swarm of bees agitated by the intoxication of honey.
Just as the female cakora bird, longing for nectar and eager for her beloved cātaka, falls incessantly upon a lotus when she encounters a cloud, so too [does the mind fall]. (23)
Or like a cow that has recently calved, which remains attached to her calf;
or like a female deer with fresh grass. (24)
Carnivorous beasts, having obtained meat, are like those afflicted by thirst at the sight of water;
the female swan is drawn by the sight of a lotus stalk, and the ant by its greed for honey.
If one's own lineage is fickle and one's mind is deluded by conceptualization, then, having raised the root of the arms, the garment is cast away once again. (26)
Agitated as they revealed their private limbs by turning back the hems of their garments,
they loosened their clothes under the pretext of scratching.
She revealed the ground as far as the edge of her breasts, and then withdrew; with the fall of her faltering pair of feet, she fell and then rose again. (28)
Under the pretext of her friends, she whispered from ear to ear in a manner that was captivating;
through the application of such affection, this was a secret fabrication of desire.
"Look, O fair-hipped one, at this mark of the moon upon your breasts"—with such words, she was filled with emotion, yet devoid of shame or modesty. (30)
Her heart unable to endure desire, whether she stands far away or nearby,
her lower lip quivering with curiosity, she seeks him out either through the mouth of a messenger or by means of letters.
Who are you? Whose son are you? Or from where have you come? For what purpose are you here? What is your undertaking? Or what is it that you desire? Speak.
Even after drinking [the world] down to the hair on his big toe, he is not satiated;
then, being skilled in that state of being, [he offers it] into the fire of the awakening of existence.
Having placed the remnants of the oblation, which are captivating to his own mind, upon her, and remaining there, he should cause agitation before her like another God of Love. (34)
On a Tuesday, one should bring kula-sindūra to the site of the funeral pyre;
having fashioned a yantra from that very kula-wood, [one should place it] within it.
Then, one should write "spheṃ [sphreṃ sphreṃ] spheṃ kiṭikiṭi" twice, followed by the mantra of Caṇḍī;
thereafter, one should write the nine-syllabled mantra of Mahiṣamardinī upon the leaf. (36)
Outside of that, having drawn the one called Jayadurgā, the Bhairavī of the cremation ground,
he should then worship Bhadrakālī at night with a concentrated mind.
Having taken his stand in the direction known as Kāmākhyā and having meditated upon the body as the digit of desire (kāmakalā),
the Kulakaulika remains naked, with all his hair fallen away.
One should meditate upon Kālī, whose mouth is formidable, whose eyes are set between her bared fangs,
who wears a girdle formed by a row of throbbing human hands, and who is naked.
Seated in the vīrāsana posture, standing upon Mahākāla, [surrounded by a garland],
with the corners of her mouth smeared by the root of the Vedas, she utters fierce cries.
She was smeared with blood dripping from a garland of severed heads, possessed full breasts,
and caused the entire earth to tremble as she struck her broad hips, which were fragrant with wine.
In her left hand she holds a sword and severed heads, while her right hand displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she has a terrifying face and a flickering tongue.
She has an ornament on her left ear adorned with the feathers of birds;
she is attended by jackals with terrifying cries; she has arisen at the time of universal dissolution (or, she has arisen from the *praṇava*). || 43 ||
With terrifying, fierce laughter, fierce roars, and fierce brandishings,
they held human skeletons and were intent on shouts of victory.

Having thus meditated upon that supreme Kālikā, who is served by those who attend the streams of all perfected ones (siddhas), the leader should worship her for the sake of attaining the Kula-perfection. 45.
Without entering the openings for penetrating into the city of another,
no Kula-siddhi whatsoever arises, not even in the slightest degree.
When even when merely thought of with ease, she bestows all accomplishments;
therefore, she is celebrated in the three worlds by the name Dakṣiṇā.

Then, O Bhairava, having addressed eight hundred [beings] for the sake of accomplishment, one should [use] the white substance with the Kālī-mantra, which is strung together with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), and so forth. (48)
Having dismissed the Goddess and established her in his heart at the crossroads,
adorned with excellent ornaments, he should then enter the enemy's city.
Having meditated upon the Goddess at the entrance and paid homage to his lineage and the Guru,
he should take white mustard seeds in his left hand while reciting the mantra.
And where there is a covering of iron spikes and bars at the gate, one should enter there at night, fearless and free from agitation, having broken through it. || 51 ||
Having transcended the hundredfold enclosure, he may then roam at will in the stables for horses,
the stables for chariots, or in the vicinity of the temple of Kālikā.
Or else, with eyes anointed and arched,
having meditated upon the Goddess— the Vidyā who possesses dreams— he should enter the pavilion of desire.
If anyone should approach, one should not feel fear there; when asked "Who are you?", one should say, "We are heroic men. (54)
The city guardians were unable to speak, grasp, or even remember [it];
there, having circumambulated their parents, the supreme abode, [they departed].
Having drawn the yantra, one should worship it and then mutter one's own mantra;
likewise at Devīkūṭa, Uḍḍīna, Kāmarūpa, and then on the bank.
Then, when Jālandhara was completely filled, thereafter on the sacrificial ground, having placed the wheels upon these [spots], and having worshipped and prostrated before them; || 57 ||
Having recited [the mantra] eight times, ten times, a hundred times, or even a thousand times,
and having taken hold of the pedestal, one should then enter the treasury.
Having established oneself upon the ground that is free from roots, and then assuming the siddhāsana posture there,
one should place the protective seat (rakṣāpīṭha) before oneself and prostrate facing the seat.
"O illustrious one! O you who are born of perfection! O my beloved deity! You have arrived;
I shall perform the worship of the lineage—grant me the ritual offerings. (60)
Placing the son’s command upon his head, he then looks toward the ocean;
he should then bring back the family flower (or fruit and flower), as well as incense and the food offering. (61)
Having taken all that which was gathered by his hand and prepared by him alone,
he then performed worship and cooked it according to his own desire.
Taking rice grains and fish meat, as well as ghee, honey, and whatever else may be available there; || 63 ||
Then, having placed [the substance] in a vessel and made it supreme, the practitioner,
having meditated upon his own chosen deity, should offer it according to the path of the scriptures.
Having cut the fruit into two and split it apart, one should offer half to the Kula-Śakti;
having consumed half oneself, one should remain standing before her.
If no woman is available, then one should cast it into water. || 66 ||
Then, having taken up the seat and first swept the ground,
he should place it near his father and become intent on contemplating the ultimate reality.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Kulacūḍāmaṇi Tantra.
The Fifth Chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said: "O Lord! When the practitioner has fallen under the power of sleep during his nocturnal practice..."
Having quickly entered Kāmarūpa, [he reached] the pavilion of the womb of Kāmākhyā. || 1 ||

Having adorned it with various materials and placed it before him, he should draw the supreme wheel, inscribed with the names of the practitioner and the object of practice, and expanded with extensive details. || 2 ||
One who possesses desire should unite desire with that which abides in desire, which stands in the midst of desire, and which is enclosed by desire;
one should desire desire through desire, and join desire with desire by means of desire. || 3 ||
Then, having meditated, recited the mantra, and observed the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and so forth,
one should place the face of the father upon the seat of the mother according to the prescribed rite.
Seizing either a piece of cloth, or even two betel leaves,
or a kārṣāpaṇa coin, or half of that, he forcibly takes what belongs to him.
Then, proceeding by way of circumambulation, he should gradually exit;
[whether it be] the property of the city women or that of the protector.
If one departs after having taken [the consort], the practitioner becomes fallen;
their blow is a display of cleverness that brings ruin to the lineage of those who stray.
If it is performed by one who is wicked, then it will certainly perish;
through transgression, there occurs an agitation of the city and bondage, and being bound, one is utterly overcome. 8.
O Śaṅkara, one should awaken the woman residing in the city with the "Awakening from Sleep" mantra,
or else by means of another thief who is of noble birth among them.
Once they have entered, they create obstacles for the practitioner; of this there is no doubt—whether they be spirits, ghosts, piśācas, rākṣasas, or reptiles.
A kinnarī, or likewise a nāga maiden, a maiden from the netherworld (pātāla),
a vidyādharī, Bhairava, Vaṭuka, and Gaṇapa; || 11 ||
Having entered while one is asleep, the women of the city cause obstacles;
they bring about the loss of offspring, agitation, disease, and likewise expulsion.
Those who cause obstacles bring about the loss of wealth and agitation;
this is the case for the lord of the city, O Śaṅkara, if such is the cause. (13)
When the abandonment of the grass occurs, then the practitioners perish;
therefore, with every effort, the Guru should cause awakening. 14.
Protection must be performed with great effort; thereafter, one should drive in the ritual stakes (kīlakas):
the thunderbolt (vajra), the spear (śakti), the staff (daṇḍa), the sword (khaḍga), the noose (pāśa), and the goad (aṅkuśa).
There, one should diligently perform the worship of the lords of those directions;
O God, [the offerings should be] flour-cakes, plantains, sweetmeats, and likewise milk-rice.
Then [offer] cooked rice, parched grain, and a bite-sized morsel, as well as coconut fruit to Viṣṇu; and to Gaṇeśa, offer sweet milk-rice and a pedestal.
Having offered a sweetmeat (modaka), a coconut, a plantain fruit, and that which is known as *lasa*,
as well as a black goat to the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa), one should then recite the Vīra-mantra.
Having recited [the mantra] and taken up a clod of earth, he should cast it in the ten directions,
just as when a horse is consecrated in a sacrifice by Śakra and the other gods.
O Maheśvara, in that same way, an obstacle is placed upon the family;
one should cause the Kula-conch to be deposited in the northeast corner of the bedchamber.
Having made it one span wide at the top and the same width at the bottom,
the practitioner should worship the King of Yantras there at night.
O Lord! How can a practitioner not wander at night and worship the Kula at night, and yet become a Kaulika? || 22 ||
Having entered the householder stage of life, being composed, he should remain at each door at night reciting the discourse on family tradition concerning the Mistress of the Three Worlds. (23)
Having bowed and [having written] the yantra, one should worship it and recite the mantra whenever the prior power has arisen.
Having bathed in the morning, one should bow to the Guru, as well as to the ancestors, the gods, and the sages. (24)

Having gratified them according to one's ability, one should worship them, permeated by a spirit of devotion; thereafter, for the sake of serving the young women of the city lord, whatever may be done under some pretext. || 25 ||
Just as it occurs there through the pretext of mingling in conversation with city women, or likewise through substances and so forth, O Bhairava! (26)

Even though she performs what is pleasing for those who act contrary to her will—such as male and female slaves—what kind of compassion does she have toward him [the Lord] by way of mere designation? (27)
The state of being a city (purabhāva) must be diligently recognized by the practitioners of the Kula; by some pretext or other, one should [attain] the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi* from oneself. (28)
Having taken [the materials] in a vessel of gold, or copper, or one known as *kula*, and having inscribed either his own *yantra* or a *kula-yantra*; || 29 ||
Either a Śrī-yantra, or a Gandharva-yantra— which is difficult for even Gandharvas to obtain— supported by ritual substances;
in its center, it should be inscribed with the name of the Kula and one's own names.
On the side, the best of practitioners, devoted to the Kula tradition, should worship the seed-syllable of Kāmakalā encircled by his own mantra.
Devoid of external signs such as family worship and the like, yet devoted to Viṣṇu; whether walking, eating, bowing, or even stumbling, he is solely intent upon Viṣṇu. || 32 ||

Victory to you, O Viṣṇu, O Hari, O Brahman! I am to be remembered by those well-born in their lineage through the extensive expansion of my names today, whether in the forest or by a body of water. (33)
Then, in the manner previously described, one should perform the agitation of the *kula*.
Thereafter, at night, in an empty house, a garden, or a temple, [one should proceed]. (34)
Having brought the goddess of noble birth, one should initiate her with the root mantra. Then, in the manner previously described, one should perform the arousal of the *kula* (or begin it). || 35 ||
If success is not attained by doing thus, one should practice the root mantra;
Kāmarūpa, the supreme seat among all seats, yields great fruit. (36)
In that regard, O Maheśvara, whatever worship is performed there even once—setting aside all other sacred seats—I dwell there within his body, my son. (37)
Therefore, the Yonimaṇḍala known as Kāmākhya is said to be a hundred times superior to them;
O Mahādeva! what more need be said now regarding their fruit? (38)
There, the primordial Mahiṣamardinī dwells together with hosts of crores;
that sacred seat (pīṭha) is the mouth of Brahmā, secret and bestowing all happiness. (39)
Since gods and goddesses, as well as sages and ascetics born of existence,
all manifest here, this family is therefore always protected by the great families.
O Maheśvara, that pīṭha is indeed twofold: secret and manifest.
The secret one is more meritorious than the manifest; it is difficult to attain even for the most excellent of practitioners. (41)
O Lord of Gods! It is hidden everywhere, yet it is obtained by those who are beautiful in their lineage (Kulasundaras). || 42 ||
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods, O You who cause creation and destruction! If I am indeed Your son, then proclaim to me the independent procedure for magnetizing.
The Goddess said:
"Listen, my son! To the supreme Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) which effects attraction;
by the mere propitiation of which a man shall certainly attract even the gods. [44]
Brahmā, joined with Sarasvatī and united with the face of the deity, surrounded by heroic powers (or:
surrounded by seed-syllables and powers), the Kālī-mantra is proclaimed. || 45 ||
O Bhairava! Having recited it once, twice, or even thrice, one can at will attract anything, whether stationary or moving, and so forth.
This Vidyā is Mahākālī; she is remembered as more secret than the secret.
She is asleep, overcome by sleep, intoxicated, bewildered, bowed down, and likewise intent on putting others to flight. (47)
Kulasundarī is bound by the entire web of defects;
she is the bud of night-conduct, day-conduct, and twilight-conduct.
One should contemplate the union of the seed-syllable and the yoga itself;
having understood this, the wise one should awaken [the disciple], for in this matter the Guru is the sole cause. (49)
The rule is to be understood as applying to men, and never to women; by whatever means, in whatever way, at all times, and from whatever source. (50)
Through the yoga of meditation upon women, supernatural powers (siddhis) will undoubtedly arise, just as a mountain of hidden ore is drawn forth by a magnet alone. 51.
Just as it goes out by itself, or like a sun-gem with the brilliance of the sun, or like [fire] from the rays of the sun with its clear luster. || 52 ||
Just as a cloud in the rainy season causes the moonstone to melt;
just as a man afflicted by hunger becomes satisfied by drinking milk when satiated by the sprinkling of water;
and just as a *gandharva* is delighted merely by the sight of flowers.
Just as the perfection of mantra (*mantrasiddhi*) occurs through the mere service of the Guru;
just as one becomes a Lord of Siddhas (*siddheśvara*) through meditation on the Great Lotus Grove (*mahāpadmavana*);
and just as enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*) occur by the mere contemplation of Tripura—[so too] they declare that the earth is filled with the essence of the flavors (*rasa*).
Just as enjoyment and liberation may occur by the mere sight of the Flower, and just as one becomes a Lord of Siddhis through the grace of Mahādurgā; || 54 ||
Just as joy arises through faith in the flowers of the family,
just as one becomes free from sin by the mere remembrance of the Gaṅgā,
and just as Śiva himself is produced by the mere act of drawing [the water], so too [is liberation attained]. || 55 ||
Just as she becomes a granter of boons by the mere thought of her,
therefore, with every effort, one should initiate one's own Kaulika woman.
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), the Uṣṇih meter,
and the deity is the southern goddess Kālikā, who bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life. || 57 ||
First, the seed-syllable is the supreme power (parā-śakti); by means of the seed-syllable, one should conceive the form.
By means of the seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels, one should perform the conception of the limbs and so forth.
Then, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) by dividing the letters of the Mātṛkā individually according to fourteen parts,
[placing them] in the heart, the two hands, and the pair of feet.
Then, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-vinyāsa*) with the fifty-syllable root mantra;
furthermore, one should practice the fivefold meditation in a single place as previously described.
One should perform the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha-pūjā) upon the ten and five lotuses [that is, upon the ten lotuses of yoga].
Having invoked the Goddess there, one should worship her, the southern ornament of the Kula.
One should worship Mahākāla afterwards, and then one should worship the power of the seat (pīṭhaśakti);
Kālī, Kapālinī, and Kullā in the first triangle.
Kurukullā, Virodhinī, and likewise Vipracittā;
Ugramukhī, Ugraprabhā, and likewise Pradīptā. (63)
One should worship Nīlā, Ghanā, Balākā, Sitā, Dhātrī, and Mudrikā,
as well as Brahmāṇī and the others, in order on the outer eastern petal.
Having done thus, one should recite the mantra while eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the day, remaining pure;
likewise at night, one should recite it a hundred thousand times, devoted to great purity.
In this matter, there is neither worship nor even consideration for other women;
by the mere recitation of mantras at night, the Dakṣiṇā shall become the bestower of perfection.

Having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and meditated upon the Goddess, the wise one should recite the mantra of Mahākālī, who brings great prosperity, in a forest or at night. 67.
When Viśvarūpiṇī is worshipped according to this very procedure,
she shall attract a celestial maiden or a Naga maiden from the netherworld (pātāla).
Araṇyā and Mahākālī are declared to be this second [form];
[one should perform] worship, meditation, ritual application, and especially recitation. (69)
All of this regarding that goddess has been proclaimed to be the same;
the recitation and all other matters previously mentioned are likewise declared here.
Araṇyā and Mahākālī shall become pure through worship;
having reached the conch in the northeast and having inscribed the yantra there, [one should proceed]. (71)
Beginning on the eighth night and concluding on the fourteenth,
a mortal, being well-restrained, should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Naked, his mouth full of betel, with disheveled hair yet having conquered his senses, his eyes rolling from intoxication upon union with another's wife. (73)
Clad in the directions (naked) and the ornament of his lineage, he who is beloved by heroes should worship with perfumes and flowers that yantra which has been drawn under whose name it was made. 74.
Afflicted by desire, she comes to that place where the worshipper is;
O child! [therein lies] wine, meat, and whatever else constitutes the Kula practice. (75)
Having given that to her, and then having offered the remainder to the Guru,
and placing his permission upon one's head, one should apply the remainder to oneself.
O child! One should perform the family worship without liquor and meat;
otherwise, the merit of a thousand lifetimes is destroyed for him. (77)
Where the offering and worship with wine is specifically prescribed,
a Brāhmaṇa should provide honey as the intoxicating liquor in copper vessels.
Alternatively, one should worship that which is honored by the Kula with Kula-liquor;
that liquor is drunk by the yogins, those foremost among the masters of yoga. (79)
That liquor which is made from molasses and flour is not fit to be drunk as an intoxicant. (80)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Kulacūḍāmaṇi Tantra.
Chapter Six. The Goddess said:
Now, O child, I shall explain to you the procedure for whatever is to be done therein:
having brought the Goddess, one should then perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-vinyāsa) upon her limbs. || 1 ||
First, the best of practitioners, having drawn the previously mentioned yantra on the summit of Devīkūṭa, should worship it according to the Kula path.
One should bow to the Goddess of the seat (pīṭha) and worship her with perfumes and flowers;
then one should worship the highly fortunate Root Goddess (mūladevī) together with her attendants (āvaraṇas).
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times there, one should then enter Uḍḍīyāna;
having worshipped her known as Yoganidrā in that seat (pīṭha), one should then perform sacrifice.
There, with a concentrated mind, one should mutter the mantra of one's own chosen deity one hundred thousand times;
then, having gone to Kāmarūpa, one should worship Kātyāyanī.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one should then worship Kāmākhyā first during the night;
thereafter, having gone to Jālandhara, one should worship Pūrṇeśī first.
There too, having recited the mantra with concentration for one hundred thousand times,
he should then go to Pūrṇagiri, worship Caṇḍī, and thereafter perform the recitation.
Having gone to the interior of Kāmarūpa, O child, one should first worship Kāmākhyā;
thereafter, at the edge, one should worship Mahādevī, the dweller of Dikkaravāsinī.

Having thus recited the mantra of Pīṭheśvarī, one should worship one's chosen deity. Having worshipped the chosen deity, one who is concentrated should recite the mantra seven hundred thousand times at night across the seven seats.
Upon the completion of the count, he should then ask: "Who are you, O Goddess, of noble lineage?
If, when this has been done, she has forgotten her own name, lineage, or birth; || 10 ||
"I am your very own chosen deity; choose an excellent boon.
Then, having prostrated before the Goddess of Gods, he should choose his own boon. (11)
If that queen does not act again as previously described,
he shall remain devoted to the service of the unshaken conduct of his clan.
Alternatively, one should worship Mahiṣamardinī in all sacred seats (pīṭhas);
then she, who is dear to the best of the Kulas, becomes pleased at her own will.
Then, having recited the root mantra, one shall become a master of all siddhis;
having gazed upon a rājavṛkṣa tree, [one should meditate on] one's chosen deity at its base.
Having performed worship during the great night (mahārātra), one should recite the mantra for three days;
O God! the best of practitioners obtains the fruit of a hundred thousand seats (lakṣapīṭha). || 15 ||
O Bhairava! [I seek] the Vetāla, the perfection of the sandals, the perfection of the sword, the collyrium, the forehead mark, the secret protection, and the Mahiṣāsuramardinī. || 16 ||
O Maheśvara! The practitioner should accomplish his desired goal through the root-mantra. || 17 ||
Bhairava said:
"O Caṇḍikā! How does the great siddhi of the Vetālas and others come to be?
O Goddess of the Gods, tell me that truth if you have affection for me. (18)
The Goddess said:
On a Tuesday at midnight, on a cremation ground marked by a corpse-seat and the four ages (yugas), the best of practitioners should take wood produced from a *bilva* or *nimba* tree. (19)
Having dug [the pit], one should indeed recite the mantra of Mahiṣamardinī eight hundred thousand times;
O dear one, one should then perform a thousand oblations right there in that cremation ground.
Having extracted a piece of wood marked with the sign of a staff and sandals from that very place,
one should go to a cremation ground on the night of the eighth day of Durgā and deposit it there.
Having placed a corpse upon it and worshipped according to the ritual,
the hero, seated upon the corpse-throne, should recite the mantra eight thousand times.
Then, having offered the *mātṛbali* sacrifice, one should consecrate the wooden staff with this mantra:
"Sphreṃ! O Staff, O highly fortunate one, beloved of the heart of the Yoginīs! (23)
"O Lord, you are held in my hand! Obey my command!
Having thus addressed the Vetāla, wherever he is employed, [he follows].
Having then reduced each of those [parts] to powder, the Kaulika returns once more, saying:
"Go, go, O highly fortunate one! O sandals of excellent complexion! (25)
By the mere touch of my foot, go a hundred yojanas,
having reached the sword-armed Aṣṭaloha, which is fifty finger-breadths in size.
Having fashioned a sword and having drawn the yantra upon it, one should offer oblations and recite the mantra;
then, having recited it a thousand times over a great corpse, [one should proceed]. (27)

Having dug [a pit], one should bind it to the tip of a seed-tree and perform the protection; then, being composed, one should cause [the corpse] to be dried at midnight on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight in the midst of a funeral pyre. || 28 ||
Then, having addressed them with affection, one should offer oblations in the cremation ground (pitṛvana),
using bilva leaves combined with the three sweets (madhuratrika).
From the feet up to the top of the head, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), one should present the bali offering;
at the end of the bali, the supreme Māyā, the goddess Mahiṣamardinī [is worshipped].
She approaches with her mouth full of offerings, her hand extended, and intoxicated with passion;
at the sound "Take it, my child," she indeed raises and brandishes her sword.
O Ghoradaṃṣṭrā! O Mahākālī! O you whose very form is the sword! KĀMŪ! O auspicious one, bring about the extensive destruction of my adversaries! 32.
Having thus addressed the sword, whichever person one hurls it at,
it cuts again and again, and having cut, it moves forward and is drawn back once more.
Alternatively, one should cut a black cat with a single blow and then bury it at night at a crossroads on a Tuesday, having consecrated it with mantras.
Having placed a plantain fruit there, one should eat sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) until a leaf emerges; then, remaining fearless, one should recite [the mantra] every night. (35)
Alone and without a lamp, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times;
then, observing that a leaf has emerged, one should cut it and bring it back free from any holes.
Having eaten sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) there on the bank of the river that day,
he should bring him [the disciple] along with his circle of friends and wash him while reciting the mantra.
O child! When that bone moves toward that stream, one should bring it there and worship Kālikā, who possesses a terrible roar.
Having recited the Kālī mantra a thousand times with a concentrated mind, the practitioner becomes a perfected master of the mantra; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (39)
Having mixed sandalwood, agallochum, and musk with bone-ash and applied it as a tilaka according to the prescribed rite after performing worship, the practitioner conquers everything.

O Maheśvara, O Lord of the Kula! Having diligently brought the fish of the Kula, the root of the Kula, the wealth of the Kula, the wine of the Kula, the food of the Kula, and the wine of the Kula to the place of the Kula, one should offer them to the Goddess.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand and eight times while standing upon the ground,
a cavity is produced there in the earth by a mere blowing upon it.
Whether the object to be accomplished is situated a hundred yojanas away,
he who glides along the surface of the earth goes to that very place.
In this way, even when encountering the contraction of his body within a narrow opening, a window, or a hollow, a man passes through unimpaired.
"O child, O Lord of Kulanātha! Without the Durgā mantra and likewise the Kālī mantra, the supernatural powers (siddhis) never arise in any way whatsoever. (45)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Kulacūḍāmaṇi Tantra.
The Seventh Chapter. Bhairava said:
"O Mother, tell me the secret convention (saṃketa) of Mahiṣamardinī."
For the perfect accomplishment of family tradition, and for the attainment of worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 1 ||
The Goddess said:
She who is the Great Sovereign (Maheśvarī), the primordial source of creation, preservation, and destruction, must be guarded with every effort; listen, for I shall tell it to you. (2)
At the end of the seed-syllable of the three worlds, there is the vocative case; then follow the two syllables of creation and destruction: this is the Vidyā Mahiṣamardinī. (3)
She is the most profound secret, eternal, the ordainer of creation and maintenance,
the seed of all gods and all accomplishments, and the everlasting one.
If it is told to one who is extremely devoted and pure,
then the eight syllables should be spoken, but neither the seed-syllable nor the means of accomplishment.
The common science of vital breath (prāṇavidyā) is Hṛllekhā, whose domain is spiritual accomplishment (siddhi).
This goddess, situated at the beginning, destroys the success of the guru.
Especially in the Kali age, she bestows a great stream of accomplishments;
yet she also inflicts a great curse upon gurus and lords of the lineage.
Jayā, Durgā, and Abhayā are proclaimed as the supreme one who rides upon a lion;
she is the seed of the three worlds, and at the end, she is the supreme crusher of the Kula.
It is better that the beloved of Fire (Svāhā) be given when joined with *yuk*, but she should not be given when accompanied by *namaḥ*.
Furthermore, the supreme Vidyā should be given when joined with *ṅe* and endowed with the Heart-mantra.
O knower of the family scriptures! [This mantra] bestows a great curse everywhere;
therefore, this nine-syllabled [mantra] must be protected with every effort.
One should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times and then perform a fire offering (homa) with one-tenth of that number.
Nārada is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and the Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chandas). || 11 ||
The deity Mahiṣaghnī is the primordial seed, both transcendent and immanent;
one should meditate upon Kālī, who is intent on the passion and intoxication of the battle with the great Daitya.
In the right hands, he holds a discus, a sword, an arrow, and likewise a trident;
in the left hands, a sword, a shield, a bow, and a raised index finger.
Wearing a yellow garment, the goddess sat upon the broad hump of a great buffalo as dark as Time itself, her two breasts full and elevated. (14)
[One should worship her] who is richly adorned with the splendor of a crown of matted locks and who brings happiness to the realm of the ancestors:
"Oṃ mahiṣahiṃsake hūṃ phaṭ, obeisance to the heart"—this is for the heart;
"Oṃ mahiṣa(daitya)śatro hūṃ phaṭ"—this is declared for the head. (15)
Oṃ mahiṣaṃ heṣaya heṣaya hūṃ (phaṭ). This is declared to be the crest-mantra (śikhāmantra). || 16 ||
Oṃ, slay, slay the buffalo! O Goddess, hūṃ phaṭ! This is also the armor mantra.
O Bhairava, hear now the weapons mantras for Mahiṣamardinī: hūṃ phaṭ! 17.
On the eight petals, one should worship the goddesses beginning with Durgā, preceded by the long vowels;
on the tips of the Palāśa leaves, one should worship the weapons in sequence, using the syllables beginning with *ya*.

Then, one who has mastered the mantras should perform the ritual application of the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī, followed by the world-protectors (lokapālas) on the outside, and then their weapons. (19)
In the ritual application, the rule for the oblation is one thousand [times], equal to the number of the Vasus.
This is a great lore; it must not be given to just anyone.
If, by the power of fortune, those of the highest lineage obtain a Kuladevī who is initiated and born of the Kula, she alone— and no other— bestows spiritual perfection.
The Hymn to Mahiṣamardinī.
Bhairava said:
O Caṇḍī, who has crushed the fierce Asuras of evil conduct, move within my heart!
At will, tear asunder the manifold calamities of the vital points caused by the waves of irresistible and fierce hostility;
thereby, this [place] shall become free from affliction— a forest for the incomparable lotus-feet of Śrī.
May my mind-goose rejoice for a long time, having reached the ocean of nectar that lies immediately beyond. || 22 ||

O fierce Mother! Having abandoned Nṛsiṃha— whose mane was as voluminous as the interior of the lovely Mount Sumeru, and whose hand-fingers were exceedingly powerful for rending the chest of Hiraṇya— the gods now serve Your glorious feet, which are skilled at crushing the fetters of bound souls.
Why would enemies serve the enemy of elephants? Would there not be fear for one who serves him? || 23 ||
O Caṇḍī! If even a single word or syllable concerning you has reached the interior of the ear, that very reality, which follows the nature of the Puruṣa, is sung of by Brahmā and the other gods.
Therefore, O Goddess, [you who are] the radiance of the sole abode of the essence of nectar for all the deities—
Today, honor me as one intent upon kissing your glorious lotus feet. || 24 ||

Let there be censure from men, or let it be; let there be no two-fold adherence to the conduct of the noble path, or let there be no fame; let there be no practice of worshipping Keśava and Kauśika, nor even my presence. O Mother, [let there be no service] to the abode of those who serve Brahmā, Hari, Smara’s enemy, Hutabhuj, and the foe of Daityas— [The rest of the verse is: —nor to the feet of the Lord of the Mountain, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Lotus-born, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Three-eyed One, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Earth, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Sky, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Waters, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Wind, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Sun, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Moon, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Stars, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Planets, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Constellations, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Sacrifice, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Vedas, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Mantras, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Tantras, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Yoga, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Sāṅkhya, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Dharma, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Artha, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Kāma, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Mokṣa, nor to the feet of the Lord of the World, nor to the feet of the Lord of the Universe, nor to the feet of the Lord of All, nor to the feet of the Supreme Lord. O Mother, let there be only this: the worship of the feet of the Lord of the Mountain, the feet of the Lord of the Lotus-born, the feet of the Three-eyed Lord, the feet of the Lord of the Earth, the feet of the Lord of the Sky, the feet of the Lord of the Waters, the feet of the Lord of the Wind, the feet of the Lord of the Sun, the feet of the Lord of the Moon, the feet of the Lord of the Stars, the feet of the Lord of the Planets, the feet of the Lord of the Constellations, the feet of the Lord of the Sacrifice, the feet of the Lord of the Vedas, the feet of the Lord of the Mantras, the feet of the Lord of the Tantras, the feet of the Lord of Yoga, the feet of the Lord of Sāṅkhya, the feet of the Lord of Dharma, the feet of the Lord of Artha, the feet of the Lord of Kāma, the feet of the Lord of Mokṣa, the feet of the Lord of the World, the feet of the Lord of the Universe, and the feet of the Lord of All—the Supreme Lord.]
May our mind always remain engaged in the practice of contemplating his glorious lotus feet. || 25 ||
If I have been instructed in the sequential contemplation of Your feet,
then for me who has been so instructed, what rare or difficult attainment could there be?
Therefore, O Goddess, [I pray to] Your two glorious lotus-feet, most abundantly filled with the weight of compassion.
O Kṣemaṅkarī! May [this work] spread within my mind, which is possessed of unimpaired excellence; may it be forgiven. || 26 ||
Embracing his own self, even the Lord of Beings fell into a state of madness;

yet that capable master would not have been able to effect the vast preservation of life had it not been for the flow of the essence of moonlight and sandalwood, its boldness having fallen away by fate.
It has not been tasted by the fragrance of the single lotus of Your feet, which is filled with the honey of nectar. || 27 ||

Alas, alas! O Mother, within the hollow of the heart of one like me— pierced by the roar of the ocean of beginningless delusion and rendered tasteless by the lack of immersion in the essence of Brahman-bliss—
is there anything capable of overcoming the intense mental anguish of the multitude of gods?
May this overflowing torrent of the most intense rain-clouds of the glorious aesthetic flavor of devotion flow forth forever. || 28 ||

The deity who is the triad of stainless consciousness and bliss, which dispels the darkness within the heart as it radiates forth like ten million suns from the interior of the mass of rays flashing from his feet;
May that Consciousness— which creates the world, extends its maintenance, and again dissolves creation—
whose splendor is like a dark cloud of freshly blossomed collyrium, ever abide within our hearts;
[and may we be protected] by the millions of rays of the fierce sun falling from the interior of the network of light-rays flashing from His feet.
May that Great Deity— who is the stainless bliss of consciousness pervading the heart’s darkness,
who creates the world, maintains it, and again dissolves it— ever abide within our minds, which are like vast clouds as dark as freshly crushed collyrium. Thus it is held in the *Tantrasāra*.
[The reading: || 29 ||
She who constantly embraces the Daitya— whose head is shrouded in the darkness spreading from within his mouth as he stumbles, runs, roars, and clearly emerges under the guise of a buffalo—
is that Durgā, the remover of the misery of the fortress of fear, who terrifies the hundreds of thousands of others.
May she who delights in victory prevail—she who is skilled at rending the wives of the arrogant gods.

In that ocean of the army—vast with its swelling hosts of short-necked horses, where the tips of waving shields and yak-tail fans whirled like circles, and which was filled with the rising, crooked, copper-colored spray of arrows; where the heads of wicked asuras were tossed about with arrogance by the spreading gale-like winds— [The verse continues: ...the Lord of the Gods, having struck down the host of demons, shone like the sun at the end of the aeon, having destroyed the world. (Note: This is a partial translation of a complex *śloka* describing a fierce battle scene, likely from a work such as the *Kādambarī*. The provided text fragment ends mid-verse.)
In which all the hunger and thirst of birds was set ablaze by the fragments of broken pieces [of food] falling apart.

In the space between the horns of a wild buffalo, its head bent sideways in a state of frenzy as it strikes violently with a fierce, rhythmic blow that brings an end to the shimmering sun, he bound his ears with the sounds of the musical notes (svaras), which are like the eight petals situated within the center of the eight directions (vasu-patra).
These were formed by the Mothers (Mātṛs) who, through their powers, produced the resonance.
And one should remember her being crushed on the beautiful battlefield of service, while the sky whirls with the joy of combat.
(In the *Tantrasāra*: "one should remember her being reduced to powder. || 32 ||
I salute Śivā, who holds in her upper and lower right and left hands a discus, a conch, a chopper, a shield, an arrow, a bow, a trident, and the gesture that dispels fear; she is dark-complexioned,
with her mass of hair tied up in a high topknot by a cluster of dark, rain-cloud-like locks, and with [her ornaments] slipping...
Her terrifying face shone with the repeated striking of her arms, and she was formidable with her fierce, loud laughter. || 33 ||
Thus, O Goddess, those who meditate upon your sinless form— which is worshipped by Śakra and others, including Durga— perform the shaking of the bodies of enemies and other such feats.

For those who perform the rites of immobilizing, expelling, killing, and so forth, by means of the mirror of the nectar of poetry and their intellect fixed upon the true goal, sovereignty and victory over enemies arise spontaneously. (34)

O Goddess! If those who desire liberation, wealth, and other goals quickly hear or recite this hymn— which was composed by me through the focused meditation upon the pair of your lotus feet, fashioned according to the secret instructions of the *Mantroddhāra-kulopacāra* (or, as stated in the *Tantrasāra*, your life-story)— then [they shall attain their desires].
O Mother of the worlds, victory to you; salutations! [All things] come into the hands of those who [worship you]. 35.
The Goddess said: "O Bhairava, I am pleased and delighted by your hearing of this hymn;
behold my form, which is not suitable for meditation but brings you happiness. (36)
This form is my primary manifestation, and likewise the form of Kālī;
Tripurā is proclaimed as the primordial form of Bhairavī. (37)

On a Kulavāra day, on the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) of the Kula period, and especially on the fourteenth (caturdaśī), the worship of the Yoginīs is performed there; therein, the Kula worship is paramount.
Just as Viṣṇu, when worshipped on his own lunar day, bestows desired objects, so too Durgā, when worshipped on her own lunar day, is the giver of boons. (39)
At the root of a bilva tree, in the wilderness, or even in a cremation ground,
the practitioner should offer an oblation consisting primarily of meat at the time of twilight.
While "Kālī, Kālī" was being uttered, Umā, in the form of Śiva,
arrived there in the form of a beast along with her retinue of attendants.
O ornament of the family! When, after eating, he raises his face toward the northeast and cries out with a melodious voice, that alone brings him auspiciousness; it cannot be otherwise.
One must certainly and invariably satisfy Śivā with the gift of food;
likewise, one should perform the daily śrāddha, the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana), and the libations to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa).
Likewise, this is the constant duty for those who worship their family deities (or those worthy of family service):
whoever does not worship the goddess Śivā in her animal form in a secluded place, [is at fault]. 44.
(38) By the howling of a jackal, all of that— his recitations, his ritual worship, and whatever meritorious deeds he has performed— is certainly destroyed instantly. (45)
Having received a curse and fallen into misfortune, Śivā weeps in the solitude;
O God Bhairava, where she is enjoyed by Śivā alone! 46.
In that very place, the pleasure of all the powers (śaktis) is extremely difficult to attain:
the power of beasts, the power of men, and likewise the power of birds, O Bhairava. (47)
Once worshipped, she causes even a defective rite to become endowed with merit;
therefore, that worship must be performed with every possible effort as a great undertaking. 48.
One who has encountered fear from kings and the like, or fear arising from traveling to another land,
should offer a bali-oblation after reflecting upon his auspicious and inauspicious karmas.
Accept it, O Goddess! O highly fortunate one! O Śivā, you who are the form of the fire of time!
Reveal clearly the fruit of both the auspicious and the inauspicious; accept this offering for you.
